strengths: Addresses a clear gap in benchmarking: CMARL is genuinely underexplored and MEAL is the first benchmark tailored for this setting
Thoughtful technical design with comprehensive environment validation (10 rules ensuring solvability) and procedurally generated tasks avoiding overfitting to fixed task sets
JAX-based GPU acceleration is practical, enabling training on longer task sequences than traditional CPU-bound benchmarks

Well-designed evaluation with clearly defined metrics (Average Performance, Forgetting, Plasticity) appropriate for continual learning, including proper ablation study identifying multi-head architectures as critical
Strong reproducibility with extensive implementation details in appendices, seed-controllable procedural generation, and complete hyperparameter specifications
Comprehensive plasticity degradation analysis (Section 5.6) demonstrating that MEAL exhibits known pathologies from single-agent continual learning
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging scope constraints (fully observable, 2-agent, discrete actions, layout-only task changes)
weaknesses: Extremely narrow domain scope severely limits generalizability: only Overcooked with layout changes; no dynamics variation, partner changes, agent count scaling, partial observability, or competitive settings tested

Disconnect between abstract claims and actual experiments: claims 'sequences of 100 tasks' but main experiments use only 20 tasks; longer sequences critical for continual learning research, making 20 tasks relatively short

Limited novelty and shallow analytical insights: purely empirical/engineering contribution with no new methods proposed; results mostly confirm expected outcome (naive CL+MARL combinations fail) without mechanistic explanation of why inter-agent conventions break down or how to address it

Only tests one MARL algorithm (IPPO): missing comparisons with value decomposition methods (QMIX, VDN), communication-enabled approaches, curriculum learning, or memory-augmented methods despite coordination being central to the problem
Normalization scheme underestimates performance where agents parallelize work—exactly where cooperation matters most; paper acknowledges but doesn't explore implications for result interpretation
Task-incremental learning only: doesn't explore class-incremental, domain-incremental, or other continual learning paradigms, limiting scope further

Questionable experimental findings warrant deeper investigation: task ID having negligible effect (Figure 5) is counterintuitive; CNN catastrophic failure on small grids seems like implementation choice; Level 3 performance (~0.2) suggests methods may not reliably solve harder tasks

GitHub repository URL not provided; some hyperparameter choices appear arbitrary (λ values of 10^11, 10^9, 10^7) without sensitivity analysis; wall-clock timing comparisons absent despite acceleration claims

strengths: Addresses genuine research gap at intersection of continual and multi-agent RL, which is underexplored
Useful technical contribution: JAX-based GPU acceleration enables training on 100-task sequences vs. 5-15 in prior CPU-bound benchmarks
Thoughtful benchmark design with procedural generation, formal solvability validation, and three principled difficulty levels
Comprehensive evaluation methodology with clear metrics (Average Performance, Forgetting, Plasticity) and detailed implementation documentation
High reproducibility standards: code on GitHub, full hyperparameters, controlled seeds, clear experimental setup
Honest limitations discussion that acknowledges scope constraints (2 agents, full observability, layout-only variation)
weaknesses: Limited scientific novelty: primarily an engineering contribution (JAX implementation + Overcooked variants) without algorithmic innovation or new understanding of CMARL challenges

Extremely narrow scope: single domain (Overcooked variants only) despite procedural generation; paper acknowledges it doesn't capture real-world complexity (language, negotiation, long-horizon planning)
Shallow experimental analysis: no mechanistic investigation of *why* methods fail on harder tasks; Figure 4 shows catastrophic forgetting but lacks root cause analysis
Ablation studies only on Level 1 (easy tasks where methods work); critical question of what matters on Level 3 (where everything fails) remains unanswered
Expected findings without compensation: 'existing methods fail to scale' is predictable; paper identifies problems but proposes no solutions or design principles for future work
Limited multi-agent specificity: all experiments use only IPPO; no evaluation with VDN, QMIX, MAPPO or investigation of how agents develop/lose coordination strategies
Single-algorithm evaluation with no analysis of learned policies, role specialization, or how implicit conventions degrade—core to the continual MARL claim
Plasticity analysis (Section 5.6) merely confirms known single-agent CL phenomena (Abbas et al., Dohare et al.); provides no new insights specific to multi-agent settings
Questionable evaluation design: single-agent normalization methodology lacks validation; limited baselines (no meta-learning or ensemble methods); no statistical significance testing
Motivation-benchmark mismatch: introduction motivates with partial observability, continuous actions, dynamic environments, yet benchmark has none of these
Limited actionable impact: benchmark is constrained enough that generalizability to other domains/settings is uncertain, limiting research value for broader CMARL community

strengths: First dedicated benchmark for continual multi-agent RL, addressing a genuine gap in the literature
Strong technical execution: JAX-based GPU acceleration enables 20-100 task sequences vs. 5-15 previously, with careful procedural generation and deterministic validation
Rigorous experimental methodology: proper statistical reporting (5 seeds, 95% CIs), well-defined metrics (Average Performance, Forgetting, Plasticity), and comprehensive hyperparameter documentation
Actionable empirical finding: multi-head architecture is critical—removing it devastates performance across all methods, suggesting task-specific output separation is essential for CMARL
Excellent reproducibility: code promised on GitHub, extensive appendices with generator/validator details, and procedurally generated tasks controllable via random seed
Honest limitations discussion that clearly identifies scope constraints (fully observable, 2-agent, discrete, task-incremental only) without overclaiming
weaknesses: Limited scope restricts impact: only Overcooked tested (despite procedural variation), restricted to 2 agents, fully observable, discrete actions; excludes competitive, partially observable, or many-agent settings; only task-incremental learning evaluated

Insufficient baseline coverage: only 5 single-agent CL methods evaluated; missing recent meta-learning approaches and MARL-specific continual learning methods; cannot assess whether failures are due to CL+MARL mismatch vs. method design

Shallow analysis of key architectural finding: multi-head importance identified but not deeply explored—no investigation of why task-specific output separation helps, or comparison of alternative multi-head designs
Incomplete results presentation: Level 2 and 3 results relegated to appendix; harder difficulty levels should appear in main text to demonstrate benchmark utility across complexity spectrum

Limited algorithmic contribution: paper identifies problems (catastrophic forgetting, coordination breakdown) but proposes no solutions; findings confirm expected behavior without advancing methodology
Missing qualitative analysis: no rollout visualizations, behavioral breakdowns, or investigation of how coordination fails; limited exploration of failure modes beyond forgetting metrics
Normalization metric underspecified: single-agent cook-deliver cycle estimate may have domain-specific biases; impact on method ranking unclear despite acknowledgment of multi-agent underestimation
Plasticity degradation analyzed only on FT baseline; unclear if findings generalize or are specific to IPPO hyperparameters
Presentation issues: Table 1 appears twice, notation could be clearer, Figure 4 caption mislabeled; normalization metric explanation buried in appendix

strengths: Addresses genuine gap: First benchmark specifically designed for continual multi-agent RL
Practical impact: First end-to-end GPU-accelerated continual RL library enabling efficient training on 100+ task sequences (hours vs. days)
Rigorous experimental evaluation: 6 baselines, 3 difficulty levels, 5 seeds, comprehensive ablations, and honest confidence intervals
Sound technical design: Well-validated procedural generation pipeline with 10 explicit solvability criteria; proper normalization for variable-sized environments
Key insights: Identifies multi-head architectures as critical; demonstrates plasticity loss in multi-agent settings; reveals existing methods fail on complex coordination tasks
Reproducibility: Extensive hyperparameter documentation, implementation details in appendices, clear experimental protocol
Well-executed engineering: Clean integration of JAX/JaxMARL with continual learning metrics; comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Severely limited domain scope: Single environment (Overcooked) with only layout variation; no variation in partner agents or environment dynamics; discrete actions only; 2-3 agents maximum; omits real-world complexity (language, negotiation, planning)

Restricted continual learning setting: Task-incremental paradigm with known task identity during training/evaluation more restrictive than class/domain-incremental; layout changes only, not partner or dynamics shifts

Limited algorithmic coverage: Only IPPO/PPO tested as base MARL algorithm; MAPPO underperformance explanation is cursory; no evaluation of value decomposition methods (VDN, QMIX) or recent MARL algorithms
Performance calibration concerns: Level 1 too easy (EWC: 0.839 with 0.031 forgetting), Level 3 too hard (best: 0.306); poorly calibrated difficulty may limit ability to discriminate methods

Limited novelty: Contribution is primarily engineering (integration) rather than algorithmic or theoretical; individual components (Overcooked, procedural generation, JAX, CL metrics) are existing work

Incomplete experimental design: Key findings relegated to appendices (curriculum learning shows 2x improvement, designated roles, PO variants); no isolated comparison of MARL-specific vs. continual learning challenges

Methodological limitations: Normalization upper bound underestimates multi-agent throughput (acknowledged); forward transfer requires expensive single-task baselines; task-identity assumption unrealistic for many applications
Hyperparameter concerns: Extreme λ values (10^11, 10^9, 10^7) for CL methods lack sensitivity analysis; unclear if results robust to these choices

strengths: Addresses understudied intersection of continual learning and cooperative multi-agent RL with clear motivation
JAX-based GPU acceleration is well-engineered, enabling efficient training on 100-task sequences (genuine practical improvement over CPU-based benchmarks)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation including six CL methods across difficulty levels with thorough ablation studies identifying critical components (multi-head architecture)
Procedurally generated environments ensure task diversity and reproducibility with formal solvability validation
Detailed hyperparameters, methodology appendices, and reproducible seeded generation support transparency
weaknesses: Benchmark limited to single, extremely narrow domain (2-agent Overcooked with small grids 6×11 max) making generalization claims unsupported—single-domain benchmarks cannot justify broad 'continual multi-agent RL' claims
No algorithmic contributions or proposed solutions; paper merely shows existing methods fail on hard tasks without investigating why or proposing fixes

Poor performance on hard tasks (Level 3: best method achieves 0.306 average, learning stalls after task 15) severely limits benchmark utility, but unclear if this reflects fundamental CMARL difficulty or poor benchmark calibration
Task-incremental learning paradigm (task identity known) is unrealistic and conflicts with standard continual learning definition; no evaluation of class/domain-incremental settings

Critical design choices reduce relevance: fully observable by default, dense reward shaping required (sparse fails catastrophically per Table 5), only 2 agents (3-agent performance degrades), requiring architectural workarounds (multi-head outputs) suggests benchmark is artificial

Inconsistent experimental setup: regularization coefficients differ 4 orders of magnitude (10^11 vs 10^7), different optimizers per method (PPO vs IPPO), hyperparameters appear untuned, making it unclear if poor performance reflects algorithmic or tuning issues

Weak forward transfer results (Table 2, negative on most methods) lack mechanistic explanation—no analysis of why knowledge fails to transfer, which task features could enable transfer, or how task similarity affects transferability
Multi-head ablation (Figure 6) shows devastating performance drop when removed, suggesting benchmark requires architectural workarounds rather than identifying what CL methods should actually do

Missing critical baselines: no single-task upper bounds for calibration, no cross-difficulty transfer analysis (Level 1→Level 3), no visualization of learned behaviors, no comparison with domain-specific CMARL methods

Limited statistical rigor: only 5 seeds with overlapping confidence intervals (Tables 10-12), no significance tests, no multiple comparison corrections, large confidence intervals on harder levels limit conclusions

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: first benchmark for continual multi-agent RL, combining two underexplored areas
Technically sound: rigorous procedural generator with 10 validation rules, appropriate metrics, comprehensive hyperparameter specification
JAX-based GPU acceleration is valuable technical contribution enabling 100-task sequences (vs. 5-15 in prior work)
Comprehensive experiments: 6 CL methods across 3 difficulty levels, ablations, N-agent studies, plasticity analysis, proper statistical reporting
Useful empirical finding: multi-head architectures critical for CMARL performance
Excellent reproducibility: promised code release, deterministic generation, controlled random seeds
Strong presentation: clear motivation, well-organized, effective visualizations, detailed appendices
weaknesses: Limited domain scope: restricted to Overcooked with primarily 2 agents; generalizability to other cooperative domains unclear; applicability to real-world use cases (AVs, warehouse robots) not demonstrated

Difficulty calibration concerns: Level 3 shows severe degradation (avg score ~0.2, learning stalls after task 15); unclear whether benchmark is appropriately calibrated or if this reveals fundamental method limitations
Task-incremental setting assumes known task identity, limiting applicability to more challenging class-incremental or task-agnostic scenarios
Limited mechanistic insights: documents that methods fail but provides insufficient analysis of why; multi-head architecture explanation is suggestive rather than definitive
No novel algorithmic contributions: purely evaluative paper implementing existing methods; would benefit from preliminary CMARL-specific algorithmic explorations
Partial observability results puzzling and incompletely explained: MAPPO underperformance in CL setting warrants deeper investigation
Difficulty level design choices appear somewhat arbitrary (width ranges, obstacle densities); sensitivity analysis or ablation studies missing
N-agent scalability issues: 3-agent results show collapse; unclear whether this motivates better multi-agent methods or indicates benchmark limitations
